title: Monitor saphyr health and consider other dependencies
description: I noticed your used saphyr which I am a big fan of too and used as well, but I was going to suggest keeping an eye on that dependency as it seems to be going stale with very little activity in the last 6 months and issues / PRs beginning to pile up. The granit-parser maintainer has been really fast to action any issues I've had with it.

title: Preserve unsupported core-schema tags as metadata
description:
## Summary

`py-yaml12` currently rejects PyYAML-generated object tags such as:

```yaml
!!python/object:__main__.DangerousPayload {}
```

That rejection is correct under YAML 1.2 core schema rules, since this is not a valid core-schema tag. But for interoperability, it would be useful for `py-yaml12` to accept the file and preserve the unknown tag as metadata, without normalizing it or executing anything.

## Reprex

```python
import yaml
from yaml12 import read_yaml

class DangerousPayload:
    def __setstate__(self, state):
        print("evaluating code")

with open("dangerous.yaml", "w") as f:
    yaml.dump(DangerousPayload(), f)
```

Current output:

```yaml
!!python/object:__main__.DangerousPayload {}
```

Then, loading that file with PyYAML can execute code:

```python
with open("dangerous.yaml") as f:
    yaml.load(f, Loader=yaml.Loader)
```

Current output:

```text
evaluating code
```

By contrast, `py-yaml12` should keep the tag as data:

```python
print(read_yaml("dangerous.yaml"))
```

Current output:

```text
ValueError: unsupported core-schema tag `tag:yaml.org,2002:python/object:__main__.DangerousPayload`
```

Intended output:

```python
Yaml(value={}, tag="!!python/object:__main__.DangerousPayload")
```

## Rationale

The current error is defensible by the letter of YAML 1.2, but it makes `py-yaml12` fail on files produced by existing YAML tooling. A more useful behavior would be to parse the document, keep the unknown tag exactly as written, and leave interpretation to explicit user code.

That keeps the safe default: loading remains data loading, not object construction or code execution. It also makes `py-yaml12` more tolerant of real-world YAML files without blessing PyYAML's object-tag behavior.

title: Great Docs site not picking up `Yaml` constructor signature
YAML 1.2 Conformance suite and specific questions
description:
Hello! I appreciate this particular effort, and I noticed you listed you were 100% compliant with the [yaml-test-suite](https://github.com/yaml/yaml-test-suite), but I wondered if you were aware of [the wider YAML Test Matrix site](https://matrix.yaml.info/)  and the related repositories: 
+ [yaml-runtimes](https://github.com/yaml/yaml-runtimes)
+ [yaml-text-matrix](https://github.com/perlpunk/yaml-test-matrix)

I read both your [In Defence of YAML](https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-05-21_in-defense-of-yaml/) article and your [YAML in 2 Minutes](https://posit-dev.github.io/py-yaml12/user-guide/yaml-in-2-minutes.html#why-yaml-12), but I am left with some questions as to the specifics that YAML 1.2 (and your implementation) addresses in the YAML 1.1 shortcomings.

### Question 1: What does py-yaml12 do with duplicate keys?

For instance, Duplicate keys are allowed in regular YAML 1.1, and YAML 1.2 states that mapping keys should be unique within a mapping. If you have duplicate keys, the behavior is undefined in the YAML 1.2 spec, and most parsers will keep the last occurrence **_or_** throw an error.
```yaml
x: cow
y: dog
x: bull
```
Not only is it unclear whether x should be "cow" or "bull" (the parser will decide 'bull', but did you know that?), if there are 200 lines between x: cow and x: bull, a user might very likely change the first x and erroneously believe that the resulting value of x has been changed - when it hasn't.

### Question 2: Does py-yaml12 presume YAML 1.2 even when there is no `%YAML 1.2`?
```
---
a: 1e2  # document["a"] == "1e2"
b: no   # document["b"] == false
```

```
%YAML 1.2
---
a: 1e2  # document["a"] == 100
b: no   # document["b"] == "no"
```
Regardless of whether YAML 1.2 has been (or will be) widely adopted, it does not help those who want to parse a JSON document with a YAML parser. JSON documents do not start with %YAML, and therefore cannot opt-in to the YAML parser behavior that would permit correct parsing of JSON.
